radio-390-red-sands.story:
Red Sands is a group of steel towers on legs in the Thames Estuary, near Whitstable in Kent, built during the Second World War as an army anti-aircraft fort and later abandoned. Forts like this were cheaper for pirate broadcasters than buying a ship, and in the 1960s several were taken over for unlicensed radio. Pirate radio existed because the BBC held a legal monopoly on British broadcasting. A station could hope to avoid prosecution only if it stood outside the three-mile territorial limit, the belt of sea a state then fully controlled.

Two weak stations used Red Sands first. Radio Invicta began in 1964, and its owner, a local fisherman, drowned that December with two colleagues when their small boat overturned in a squall on the way back to shore. Supplies ran so low the next month that the station sent out distress calls. It closed and became K-I-N-G Radio, which also failed to pay its way and approached Ted Allbeury for help. Allbeury suggested programmes modelled on women's magazines and aimed at people at home during the day. Radio 390, named after a wavelength close to its real one, started in 1965 with easy-listening music. A rival mocked it as Stone Age radio, but it became popular. The fort itself gave it a technical advantage. A 250-foot mast on an inner tower, held by cables from the outer towers, gave a 10-kilowatt transmitter good coverage of southern England, although the station told advertisers it had 35 kilowatts.

Its legal trouble came with the wider crackdown of 1966. On 25 November a magistrates' court convicted its managers of illegal broadcasting, fined them £100 and ordered the station closed. They appealed, and in December the High Court decided the case, R v Kent Justices ex parte Lye, by two judges to one. The question was where to begin measuring the three miles. A government order of 1964 allowed measurement from a low-tide elevation, a sandbank that shows only at low water. Measured from such a bank, the fort was inside the limit. The fort stayed where it was, and the legal line moved past it.

This ruling matters to anyone trying to build offshore. The location of a structure can be correct on the day it is occupied and wrong after a government changes how the line is drawn, or after a court reads an old order in a new way. Radio 390 returned on 31 December with fresh evidence that the fort lay outside the limit. Magistrates rejected that evidence in February 1967 and fined the company £200 and its directors £40 each. The station carried on. The Post Office then used a different tool, a civil court order called an injunction, which it won in May.

An appeal was refused on 28 July, because Parliament had by then passed the Marine Broadcasting Offences Act. That law made it an offence for British citizens to take part in offshore broadcasts or to supply or advertise on them, so the location of the fort no longer decided anything. It would have closed the station by 14 August in any case. Radio 390 went off the air on 28 July, just after 5 p.m., with the national anthem. Thieves raided the empty fort on 6 August and were arrested soon after.
radio-390-red-sands.why: Text read as if the station closed on 14 August. It closed on 28 July, the day the appeal failed. The raid was on 6 August, nine days later.

radio-city-shivering-sands.story:
Shivering Sands is an abandoned Second World War army fort in the Thames Estuary off England, a cluster of steel towers on legs that once stood seven strong. One tower was knocked down when a ship hit it, and another was left isolated. In the 1960s it housed Radio City, one of the unlicensed stations that broadcast pop music to Britain from just offshore, because the BBC held a monopoly on legal radio and played little of it.

The musician Screaming Lord Sutch started the station as Radio Sutch on 27 May 1964. It was a low-budget affair, with a transmitter from a Halifax bomber, car batteries for power and a scaffold pole with a skull-and-crossbones flag as an aerial. By September Sutch had tired of it and sold it to his friend and unpaid manager, Reginald Calvert, for a reported £5,000. Calvert repaired the catwalks between the towers, fixed up living quarters, built studios, and raised a tall mast on the central tower. Output never exceeded 2 kilowatts, though the station claimed 10 to attract advertisers. Part of its income came from Dutch and American religious shows that paid for airtime. The Port of London Authority complained that its signal interfered with radio links to wind and tide gauges on the isolated tower, which could put shipping at risk.

Possession of the fort depended largely on who was physically there. In September 1965 Radio City began merger talks with Radio Caroline, and a transmitter was delivered to the fort for Caroline's use. Major Oliver Smedley, a retired officer behind another station, claimed to own it. The transmitter proved unusable, the merger collapsed and nobody collected it. Calvert then explored a merger with Radio London. At 3 a.m. on 20 June 1966 seamen sent by Smedley boarded the fort and took it from the disc jockeys, intending to hold it for ransom. The next evening Calvert went to Smedley's home and was shot dead there. Smedley was charged with murder and cleared on grounds of self-defence.

The shooting was widely reported. Law professor James Grimmelmann's history says it turned public feeling against the stations and led the government to step up enforcement of the Wireless Telegraphy Act, which banned unlicensed broadcasting. It also led toward the Marine Broadcasting Offences Act of 1967. Other stations, including Roy Bates's Radio Essex, were prosecuted that autumn. It was then established, following a new reading of the rules on territorial waters, that Shivering Sands itself lay inside British waters, so existing law covered it. Radio City closed at midnight on 8 February 1967, and the national anthem was its last broadcast.

Grimmelmann also notes that Bates was linked in a vague way to a plan to seize Shivering Sands in the winter of 1967, which may have been a hoax. The case shows how a dispute over an offshore structure could turn violent when no police were on hand.
radio-city-shivering-sands.why: 'He' read as Smedley, the person just named. The man shot was Calvert.

rem-island.story:
REM Island is a steel platform built in 1964 to broadcast commercial radio and television to the Netherlands from the North Sea. At that time the Dutch had one television channel, with airtime divided among six public broadcasting groups, and advertising on it was strictly forbidden. Advertisers and viewers both wanted something else, and pirate stations on ships were already reaching several North Sea countries. REM, short for Reclame Exploitatie Maatschappij, or Advertising Operation Company, saw a market.

The company did something new. Earlier European pirates had used ships, or old military structures in Britain's case, and REM had a platform built for the purpose in the harbour of Cork, Ireland. It was towed to a spot about 10 kilometres off Noordwijk and anchored in cement on the seabed. Test broadcasts began in August 1964, and regular television started on 1 September at 6:30 in the evening with an advertisement for Johnson's Pledge furniture polish. The money came from advertising, some of it collected before the station even existed. Commercials were shot on 16mm film and spliced into imported series such as The Saint, Mister Ed and The Adventures of Robin Hood before the reels were sent out to the platform. Viewers needed a special aerial, and the station aimed at about 750,000 sets in the western Netherlands. A survey that August found 83 per cent of respondents against closing it.

Dutch law banned such broadcasts. The platform stood outside territorial waters, the coastal belt a state fully controls, so officials had no power to stop it there. The government's answer relied on a newer idea in the law of the sea, the 1958 Geneva Convention, which gave a coastal state rights over the continental shelf, the seabed off its coast. The Senate passed a law on 1 December 1964 forbidding the platform's radio and television services, and on 12 December the government put the measure into effect. Accounts of what it did differ. Wikipedia's account says it split the North Sea into continental sections and declared the seabed under the structure to be Dutch territory. An account on the site offshoreradio.info says territorial waters were not extended, and that the North Sea Installations Act made Dutch legislation apply to installations standing on the Dutch part of the continental shelf, where the Netherlands can assert economic rights such as gas and oil extraction. On that second account the water around the platform stayed outside Dutch territory, and Dutch law reached the structure because of the seabed it stood on.

The company tried to get around the law. It announced that its television operations had been sold to a British company, High Seas Television, for £100, and it transferred ownership of the island to a Panamanian company. TV Noordzee made its last transmission on 14 December. Radio Noordzee kept going until the morning of 17 December, when boats and police helicopters arrived. It went off the air at 9:07. One account says Dutch marines boarded, and another says dozens of police officers.

This is the important difference from a ship. A ship can be moved and answers to the country whose flag it flies. Something fixed to the seabed can be reached through the coastal state's rights over that seabed.

The backers formed a new company, TROS, in a final effort to survive, and a year later it came back legally as a public broadcaster. Television advertising was legalised in the Netherlands in 1967. The government used the platform to measure sea temperature and salt levels. A sale attempt failed in 2004, and it was dismantled in 2006. Since March 2011 it has stood in Amsterdam's harbour as a restaurant.
rem-island.why: Story said the stations went silent five days before the boarding. TV stopped on 14 Dec and radio ran until the raid on 17 Dec. The 'seabed declared Dutch territory' claim comes only from Wikipedia and conflicts with the account that territorial waters were not extended and the law applied to shelf installations, so both are given. Added the sale manoeuvre.
rem-island.mechanism: A state can reach a structure beyond its territorial sea by applying its law to installations standing on its part of the continental shelf, the seabed off its coast. That is why building a permanent platform gave REM less protection than a ship had.

itu-haps-definition.story:
Radio signals cross borders, so countries need a shared rulebook on who may use which frequencies. The International Telecommunication Union (ITU), the United Nations agency in Geneva that deals with radio, keeps that rulebook, called the Radio Regulations. Paragraph 1.66A of those regulations defines a high-altitude platform station as a station on an object at an altitude of 20 to 50 kilometres and at a specified, nominal, fixed point relative to the Earth. In plain words, it is a radio transmitter on something that hangs high in the sky over one spot, doing some of the work of a satellite.

The word station is the important one. The definition exists so that makers of these craft can be given frequencies. It does not describe a place where anyone may live, and it says nothing about who owns the air at that height.

The height band sits above ordinary traffic. Airliners fly lower, and the top band of controlled airspace in the United States, called Class A, ends at 60,000 feet, about 18 kilometres. Projects aimed at this band include the Airbus Zephyr, a solar-powered drone with an endurance goal of 64 days, the BAE PHASA-35, the Kea Atmos Mk1 and the Stratobus airship. Google's Loon balloons also worked in the stratosphere until the project ended in 2021.

Which law governs this height is unsettled. A 2023 dissertation at the University of Pretoria described a lack of clarity about the rules for these craft, because they sit between air law, run by national aviation authorities and the International Civil Aviation Organization, and the space treaties. No treaty fixes where a country's airspace ends, and a United Nations working group has tried to settle the question since 1984 without consensus. Australia, Denmark and Kazakhstan take the position that airspace ends at 100 kilometres, and the other lines proposed include 80 kilometres and a line based on the lowest orbit a satellite can hold. All of those are above 50 kilometres. So on any of those lines a platform in this band is still in airspace, and over a country's land or territorial sea it is in that country's airspace. Anyone hoping to found a place at 20 kilometres would find the ITU able to help with a radio licence only, and that licence is applied for through a national government.
itu-haps-definition.why: The 'unsettled' point can be narrowed. No agreed line exists, but every line in the state positions and proposals retrieved sits above the HAPS band. The last sentence is reasoning from those lines.

add_sources.t: Where does space begin, Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom, 2019

chicago-convention.story:
The Chicago Convention is the main treaty on international civil aviation. Near the end of the Second World War, governments knew that long-distance flying would soon be routine, and they wanted common rules on who may fly where. Fifty-two states signed in Chicago on 7 December 1944. It came into force on 4 April 1947, the same day the International Civil Aviation Organization, the United Nations aviation agency, began work. It now has 193 parties, including every United Nations member except Liechtenstein.

Article 1 is the rule that matters most here. Every state has complete and exclusive sovereignty, meaning supreme legal authority, over the airspace above its territory. Article 2 defines territory as a state's land and the territorial waters next to it, the coastal belt it fully controls. This continues a rule from the 1919 Paris Convention, and scholars trace both to an old Roman-law saying that whoever owns the soil owns up to the sky. A foreign aircraft has no general right to be there. Scheduled airlines need permission.

The treaty also settles what an aircraft is in law. Under Articles 17 and 18 an aircraft has the nationality of the state in which it is registered and cannot be validly registered in more than one. Article 3 limits the treaty to civil aircraft, leaving out military, customs and police aircraft. Over the open ocean beyond the coastal belt, Article 12 says the rules are those set under the Convention, so the air there is regulated even though no country owns it. A 2023 commentary on the Chinese balloon shot down by the United States noted that a balloon also counts as an aircraft under this treaty.

The treaty never says how high a state's sovereignty goes, and no later agreement has settled the height. A United Nations working group in Vienna has tried to settle it since 1984 without reaching consensus. Australia, Denmark and Kazakhstan take the position that airspace ends 100 kilometres above sea level, and some other countries follow that approach. Other proposals include 80 kilometres, the height above which the US Air Force awards astronaut wings, and a line based on the lowest orbit a satellite can hold, put at anywhere from about 100 to 160 kilometres. Each of these lines is far above the 20 to 50 kilometres where balloons and airships work. So on any of them such a craft is in airspace, and over a state's land or territorial waters it is in that state's airspace. The open question matters mainly for space planes and other craft that climb higher.

For someone hoping to found a place in the sky, this treaty closes most routes. Anything above land or territorial waters is already in a country's air and needs that country's consent. Anything above open ocean still needs a nationality and must follow the rules of the air. A platform with no registration would have no treaty right to enter anyone's airspace or land at anyone's airport.
chicago-convention.why: Open point on the height of sovereignty answered with state positions and the UN working group record. The balloon sentence was wrong to imply balloons raise the boundary question, on the lines proposed.

add_sources.t: Where does space begin, Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom, 2019

tokyo-convention-aircraft-flag.story:
The Tokyo Convention is a treaty signed in Tokyo on 14 September 1963 that settles which country's law applies to crimes on board an aircraft in flight. Before such rules, a crime over the open ocean, or over a place no country rules, could leave no one clearly responsible. The treaty fills that gap. It does not cover state aircraft used for military, customs or police work.

The answer it gives is the state of registration, the country on whose list the aircraft is entered. Article 3 says that country has power over crimes committed on board, and each party must make sure its own law provides for this. The arrangement resembles the rule for ships, which fall under the law of the country whose flag they fly. A Panama-registered aircraft over Antarctica therefore carries Panamanian criminal law inside it, and passengers cannot claim they have left all legal systems behind.

Other countries' power is limited. Article 4 allows a party that is not the country of registration to interfere with a plane in flight, to enforce its criminal law, only in a few exceptional situations. A law review article from India describes jurisdiction, meaning legal authority, as resting first with the country of registration, with other countries sharing some powers.

That arrangement left a gap, because a country where a disruptive passenger was handed over might have no power to prosecute. A 2014 amendment, the Montreal Protocol, came into force on 1 January 2020 after Nigeria became the 22nd state to ratify it. It allows prosecution in the state where the aircraft lands, among the states that have ratified it.

The treaty also deals with what happens in the cabin, since police are not on hand. The commander, the crew and in some cases passengers may act to prevent offences. The commander may restrain someone, put an offender off the plane at a landing or hand them to the authorities there.

Suppose a group built a large aircraft or airship to live on outside every country. If it is registered, the law of the registering country follows it, including over open ocean. If it refuses registration, the Chicago Convention's rules on nationality and airworthiness are not met, and other countries have reason to bar it from their airspace and airports. Registering in a small country with light rules moves the question without removing it, since the aircraft is still under one country's power.
tokyo-convention-aircraft-flag.why: Missing later development: Montreal Protocol 2014, in force 1 Jan 2020, widened jurisdiction beyond the state of registration.

add_sources.t: IATA, Montreal Protocol 2014 entry into force, 28 Nov 2019

us-v-causby.story:
United States v. Causby is a 1946 decision of the American Supreme Court on whether a landowner owns the sky above their land. It decided that a person does not, while also protecting the air close to the ground. It is on the map because it answers a tempting idea, that someone could buy a plot and claim a private domain straight up above it.

The Causby family owned 2.8 acres near an airport outside Greensboro, North Carolina, with a house and outbuildings used mainly for raising chickens. The end of a runway lay 2,220 feet from their barn. From May 1942 the American military used the airport, and bombers, transports and fighters passed over the property on their glide path, as low as 83 feet, which was 67 feet above the house and 18 feet above the highest tree. The Court recorded that planes blew old leaves off the trees and that the noise was startling. Terrified chickens flew into the walls and about 150 died, so the family gave up the chicken business. They also lost sleep.

The family argued that the government had taken their property. The Fifth Amendment to the Constitution requires payment when it does so. A lower court, the Court of Claims, agreed and valued the loss at $2,000. The government answered that Congress had declared national sovereignty over the air, with a public right of transit through navigable airspace, so there was no taking at all.

The old common-law rule, written in Latin as cujus est solum ejus est usque ad coelum, says that whoever owns the soil owns everything up to the sky. Justice Douglas, writing for the Court, said that this doctrine has no place in the modern world and that the air is a public highway. If the rule stood, every transcontinental flight would expose its operator to countless trespass suits. So the sky above the land belongs to no private owner. The owner does hold at least as much space as can be occupied or used in connection with the land, because otherwise nobody could put up a building or plant a tree. Flights count as a taking only if they are so low and so frequent as to interfere directly and immediately with the use of the land. Airspace above that level is public, and the Court declined to set the exact height.

The family therefore won on the principle, and the case went back to the lower court because its findings did not describe what had been taken. Justice Black dissented. On 5 January 1948 the Court of Claims described what had been taken as a right to fly through the air over the property at heights between 83 and 365 feet. It noted that the government had since given that right up, allowed recovery for the destroyed chickens, and entered judgment for the family for $1,435, plus 4 per cent a year for the delay in payment from 1 June 1942.

For anyone hoping to claim the air above a plot of land, the ruling limits the claim to the low air needed to use that land. Above it, the air is under the national government's control and open to traffic. A later owner gains no separate territory by building upward.
us-v-causby.why: Added how the case ended on remand.

add_sources.t: Causby v. United States, 75 F. Supp. 262 (Ct. Cl. 1948)

antarctic-claims-article-iv.story:
Antarctica is a continent of ice with no native human population, and seven countries claim parts of it, in eight separate claims. A treaty has frozen those claims since 1961. Understanding why matters to anyone who looks at the map, sees empty land and wonders whether they could claim some of it.

The claims grew mainly out of whaling and rivalry. France dates its claim to Adélie Land from 1840, when the explorer Jules Dumont d'Urville landed there and named it after his wife. Britain's dates from 1908, when it said it needed to regulate and tax whaling, and in 1917 it extended the claim toward the South Pole. In 1923 Britain created the Ross Dependency under New Zealand's governor, and in 1933 it transferred a huge sector to Australia. Norway claimed Peter I Island in 1931 and Queen Maud Land in 1939 to protect its whalers, Chile claimed a sector in 1940 and Argentina in the 1940s. Argentina and Chile also point to old Spanish grants. Most claims are slices meeting at the pole. Those of Argentina, Chile and Britain overlap, and in 1943 Britain began Operation Tabarin to put people on the ground and support its position.

The countries that made no claim saw the matter differently. In the International Geophysical Year of 1957 and 1958, a large scientific effort, 12 countries worked there. They signed the Antarctic Treaty in Washington on 1 December 1959, and it came into force on 23 June 1961. It now has 58 parties. It keeps the continent for peaceful use and science and bans military activity.

Article IV settles the dispute by pausing it. No side has to give up its position or accept anyone else's. Nothing done while the treaty is in force can support or deny a claim or create rights of sovereignty, meaning legal ownership by a state, and no new claim or enlargement can be made. A country can therefore run a station, register a birth or plant a flag without changing the legal position by a single metre. That removes the reason to race for land.

The results are unusual. Britain, France, Australia, New Zealand and Norway recognise one another's claims. Recognition stops with the claimant countries, and the United States and Russia keep the right to make claims of their own. Countries without claims, such as China and India, run research stations on land others claim. Marie Byrd Land, about 1.6 million square kilometres, remains unclaimed, though Article IV bars anyone from claiming it now. A 1991 agreement, the Madrid Protocol, added a ban on mining.

So a private person cannot acquire any of it. A new claim has no effect.
antarctic-claims-article-iv.why: 'Other countries do not recognise the claims' left out that five claimants recognise one another.

flandrensis.story:
The Grand Duchy of Flandrensis is a self-declared country with no people on its land, a kind of hobby state called a micronation. It claims five islands off West Antarctica: Siple, Cherry, Maher, Pranke and Carney. Niels Vermeersch of Belgium started it on 4 September 2008 as a two-week hobby, drawing on the medieval County of Flanders.

It grew into something closer to a club with state furniture. It had identity cards, a currency, a newspaper, a constitution, an anthem and a football team, and until 2014 it ran partly as a political simulation with parties and yearly elections. The islands lie off the part of West Antarctica that no country has claimed. Article IV of the Antarctic Treaty bars new claims, so the claim has no legal effect, and nobody has had reason to test it.

It has since described itself as an ecological project to draw attention to melting ice. In 2021 it registered in Belgium as a non-profit, which gave it a real legal form under Belgian law, and counted 741 citizens of 71 nationalities. It says it does not seek diplomatic recognition, meaning acceptance by real governments, and does not intend to visit its islands. Its founder spoke at the ChangeNOW climate summit in Paris in 2022, and the project co-hosted the first European MicroCon, a micronation meeting, at Ypres in August 2023. On 25 November 2025 it adopted a new flag, replacing the one it had used since its founding.
flandrensis.why: Later activity exists: new flag in November 2025.

talossa-antarctic-claim.story:
The Kingdom of Talossa is a self-declared country, or micronation, that began as a teenager's project in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, and that also claims a part of Antarctica. Robert Ben Madison, aged 14, founded it in his bedroom on 26 December 1979, shortly after his mother died. He took the name after finding that it means inside the house in Finnish. Through his teens he produced a handwritten newspaper, a flag and an emblem, with about a dozen relatives and friends as members.

In 1980 he began inventing a Talossan language, mostly French-based, which now claims 35,000 root words and has its own language committee. Talossa is known for the language and for its internet presence, and it has never run a territory. It has had a website since 1995. Stories in the New York Times and Wired in the mid-1990s brought in new citizens, and that web presence helped inspire later internet micronations. Madison ended his kingdom in late 2005, but Talossa kept going without him. He registered the name as a service mark and created a non-profit corporation in Wisconsin, and by 2013 the mark had been cancelled and the corporation dissolved.

Its claim covers the east side of Milwaukee, the small French island of Cezembre and part of Marie Byrd Land in Antarctica, the area no country claims. Its members live elsewhere and none on the Antarctic land. In 2000 Wired described it as one of the projects that claim territory but would not take power if offered it. Milwaukee remains under American law and Cezembre under French law. Marie Byrd Land is closed to new claims by the Antarctic Treaty.

On 5 August 2023 it counted 157 active citizens and 564 registered people in all. In December 2024 Txec Róibeard dal Nordselvá succeeded John I as its king. No state or United Nations body recognises any of the territory claimed.

westarctica.story:
The Grand Duchy of Westarctica is a self-declared country, or micronation, claiming Marie Byrd Land, about 1.6 million square kilometres of West Antarctica and the one large area no country claims. In 2001 Travis McHenry, a United States Navy intelligence specialist, read in the CIA World Factbook that no state had claimed it, and he declared the Protectorate of Westarctica. He wrote letters to many countries over the years, but only other micronations responded with recognition.

Having no land to run, the project lived on paper and online, with a flag, a coat of arms, a currency called the Ice Mark and titles of nobility. In 2004 McHenry began issuing fantasy passports as souvenirs, and he stopped after learning that a scammer in Kenya was selling them to refugees as real travel documents. By 2006 his Navy superiors knew he was writing to foreign governments and told him to choose. He kept his job and gave the title of Grand Duke to a friend, Philip Karns. After leaving the Navy he started another micronation, Calsahara, in the Californian desert, which was merged into Westarctica, and he took back the title in 2010.

In 2014 he registered Westarctica in Sacramento as a non-profit under American tax law, and it now campaigns on climate change and offers a research scholarship. It reports over 5,000 members as of 2018 and hosted a micronation meeting, MicroCon, in Las Vegas in 2022. It says a Russian polar research institute gave it permission to use an abandoned research station during a planned trip.

The risk of official-looking papers came up again. In July 2025 Indian police arrested Harsh Vardhan Jain for running a fake Westarctica embassy from a rented house in Ghaziabad, with false diplomatic number plates, fake passports and stamps, and money linked to suspected laundering. Westarctica acknowledged that he had served as its Consul-General to India while disowning the plates and documents, and it said he had been removed from its roster of representatives.

Article IV of the Antarctic Treaty forbids any new claim while the treaty is in force, so the claim has no legal standing, even over land no country has claimed. McHenry found a real gap on the map, and the treaty had closed it decades before he arrived. Westarctica continues as an online project with no one on the land.

luxembourg-space-resources-2017.story:
This is a law Luxembourg passed on 20 July 2017 saying companies can own materials they mine in space, the first such law in Europe. Luxembourg is a small European country, and in 2016 it announced a programme called SpaceResources.lu to attract space mining firms. At the time only the United States had a similar law.

Article 1 says that space resources are capable of being owned. The rest sets out how a company gets government approval for a mission and how officials supervise it. The procedures were largely modelled on those used for the financial sector. So a company would apply for a licence, much as a bank or fund does there, and then operate under supervision.

Luxembourg set out to be more open than the United States in two ways. The American law protects only United States citizens, while Luxembourg's is not tied to nationality, so a foreign-owned company with a Luxembourg base can use it. Export controls on space technology are also seen as lighter in Europe, which the law firm commentary treats as a selling point for firms that find American rules on selling hardware and hiring foreigners burdensome.

The difficulty is Article II of the Outer Space Treaty of 1967, the main international agreement on space, which bound 105 countries including Luxembourg when the law was passed. It says outer space, including the Moon and other bodies, is not subject to national appropriation by claim of sovereignty, by use or occupation, or by any other means. The treaty does not directly mention private owners or mined materials. Scholars are split on whether a country may give private property rights in what is extracted. Luxembourg's own Council of State, which advises on new laws, said in April 2017 that it was unclear whether international law allows this. The law tries to avoid the conflict by covering only the materials and saying nothing about ownership of the Moon or an asteroid. Think of a fishing licence, which covers the fish caught and not the sea.

For someone hoping to found a place in space, this law gives very little. It offers rights to what a mission brings out of the ground, and a government supervisor. It offers no land and no right to rule anything. Other countries are not bound to respect the title, since only international agreement could make them do so, and the commentary itself says domestic law will need to be complemented by international accords. One step in that direction is the Artemis Accords, drafted by NASA and the US State Department. Luxembourg was one of eight original signatories on 13 October 2020, and 78 countries had signed by 28 October 2026. Signatories affirm that extracting and using space resources does not inherently constitute national appropriation, and they state an intent to help develop international rules. Critics argue that the Accords themselves violate Article II. Countries that have not signed have made no such statement.

The two best-known asteroid mining firms of that period, Planetary Resources and Deep Space Industries, were both sold by January 2019. No court has tested the law.
luxembourg-space-resources-2017.why: The 105-party count was the 2017 figure, stated as current. Added the Artemis Accords as the main later state practice on the split the entry describes.

nemitz-eros.story:
Eros is an asteroid, a large rock orbiting the Sun. Gregory Nemitz, an aerospace consultant from Carson City, Nevada, published a claim of ownership over it in March 2000, under the name of the Eros Project for Space Property Law. He had never been there and had no plan to go. His purpose was to force a court to say whether private people can own property in space. His view, in his own words, was that there will be no commercial activities in space without official respect for private property rights.

His chance came on 12 February 2001, when NASA, the American space agency, landed its NEAR Shoemaker probe on Eros and left it there. Nemitz sent NASA an invoice for $20, the parking and storage fee for the next century. The amount was nominal. An unpaid bill gave him something he could take to court.

NASA refused to pay, with its lawyer saying the claim appeared to have no foundation in law. Nemitz then wrote to the State Department, which replied that in its view private ownership of an asteroid is precluded by Article II of the Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space. That article says that outer space and bodies in it are not subject to national appropriation by claim, use, occupation or any other means. Its words speak of national appropriation, which left open the question Nemitz wanted answered, whether a private owner is covered too.

On 3 November 2003 he filed a complaint in federal court in Reno asking for a declaratory judgment, a ruling that states what the law is without ordering payment. His question was whether the treaty rules out private ownership of asteroids or property on other bodies. The judge, Howard McKibben, ordered the case dismissed in April 2004. Nemitz appealed in July to the Ninth Circuit, a federal appeals court in San Francisco, citing a presidential commission that had just warned that uncertain property rights could strangle a space industry. The Ninth Circuit affirmed the dismissal in 2005.

Press and bloggers called this the first legal case on property in space. The district court ruled that he had failed to prove he had any property right, and the appeals court left that ruling in place. So the case shows that publishing a claim creates no right a court will enforce. It did not decide whether property in space can exist at all, and the Supreme Court has not ruled on that. A writer at Reason observed that a claimant who has never been anywhere near the asteroid is easy to distinguish from a serious miner. Its main result was a written American government position against private ownership of an asteroid. Ten years later, in 2015, Congress took a different path by giving Americans ownership of what they mine, while disclaiming any ownership of the asteroid itself.
nemitz-eros.why: Story said no ruling gave reasons and did not state the appeal result. The district court held he had failed to prove a property right, and the Ninth Circuit affirmed.

add_sources.t: Mining in the Final Frontier, Washington Journal of Law, Technology & Arts

uae-japan-space-resources.story:
These are laws from the United Arab Emirates and Japan that allow companies to use materials mined in space, following the United States in 2015 and Luxembourg in 2017. The Emirates was also working with a private Japanese company on a Moon landing planned for 2022.

The Emirates' Federal Law No. 12 of 2019 is a general space law. It covers licensing, registering spacecraft, liability and insurance, along with rules on building facilities on other planets and on using space resources. It had come into force by early 2020. Japan's parliament, the Diet, then passed Act No. 83 of 2021, on business activities in exploring and developing space resources, which made Japan the fourth country to pass such a law. Article 5 is headed Acquisition of Ownership of Space Resources. According to the news site Atalayar the law lets Japanese companies find, extract and own minerals from the surface and subsurface of the Moon, Mars or other bodies, under the umbrella of Japan's international space agreements. Japan's Hayabusa 2 mission had returned a few grams of dust from the asteroid Ryugu in December 2020, which showed that extraction is possible on a small scale.

The legal idea is that national practice can gradually shape international law. Treaties are one source of international law, and another is custom, the consistent practice of states that they treat as lawful. When several countries pass similar laws and others do not object, this can start to count as custom. Together with the American and Luxembourg laws, these acts form a growing group of countries treating mining as a lawful use of space. The Emirates and Japan were also among the eight original signatories of the Artemis Accords on 13 October 2020, and 78 countries had signed by 28 October 2026. Signatories affirm that extracting and using space resources does not inherently constitute national appropriation. Critics argue that the Accords violate the Outer Space Treaty, and the legal status of space mining remains unclear, so a rule formed in this way has not yet been established.

No international treaty authorises this. Article II of the Outer Space Treaty still bars any country from claiming a body in space, and these laws give ownership of materials and not of ground. A person living at a mine on the Moon under these laws would remain under the licensing country's supervision. No court has tested the laws.
uae-japan-space-resources.why: Added the Artemis Accords, the main evidence on the custom question the entry raises.

us-space-act-2015.story:
This is an American law, signed on 25 November 2015, that gives American companies ownership of materials they mine in space. It is Title IV of the Commercial Space Launch Competitiveness Act, and its main rule became Section 51303 of Title 51 of the United States Code. A presidential commission had warned in 2004 that uncertainty over who owns space materials could strangle a space industry at the start, since no company would invest in a product it might not legally own.

The rule is short. A United States citizen engaged in commercial recovery of an asteroid resource or a space resource is entitled to whatever is obtained, including to possess, own, transport, use and sell it, in accordance with applicable law, including the international obligations of the United States. It applies only to United States citizens. The commercial launch chapter of the same title of the Code defines a citizen to include companies organised under American law and foreign companies controlled by Americans. If that definition applies here, those companies qualify, and a foreign firm with no controlling American owner gains nothing.

It had to be written carefully because of the Outer Space Treaty of 1967, the main international agreement on space. Article I says the use of space is the province of all mankind and must benefit all countries. Article II says that outer space and bodies in it are not subject to national appropriation by claim of sovereignty, by use or occupation, or by any other means. Opinio Juris, a law blog, wrote that Congress avoided a conflict in three ways. The right goes to private citizens and not to the nation. It is subject to international obligations. And the Act states that the United States does not assert sovereignty, meaning national ownership, or exclusive rights over any body in space.

So a company could own a tonne of mined ore while nobody owned the asteroid. A familiar comparison is fishing on the high seas, where a boat owns what it catches although no one owns the ocean. The same Opinio Juris writer, who supported the law, pointed out that other countries could then do the same for their own citizens, leaving the matter to each country's rules. Critics argued that the law breaches the treaty.

Luxembourg copied the idea in 2017, and others followed. The law offers nothing to someone wanting territory. It grants no land, no settlement and no right to govern, and it expressly disclaims those things. Whether one country can grant rights that others must respect is still debated. The nearest thing to an international answer is the Artemis Accords, drafted by NASA and the US State Department and first signed on 13 October 2020. Signatories affirm that extracting and using space resources does not inherently constitute national appropriation, and 78 countries had signed by 28 October 2026. Critics argue that the Accords violate Article II and favour American and commercial mining interests. Countries that have not signed have made no such statement, and no court is known to have ruled on the question.
us-space-act-2015.why: 'Citizen' in US space law is not limited to individuals. Added the Artemis Accords as the later development on the open question.

cyprus-buffer-zone-pyla.story:
The United Nations Buffer Zone, also called the Green Line, is a strip of land patrolled by peacekeepers that runs 180 kilometres across the Mediterranean island of Cyprus. It covers 346 square kilometres and ranges from under 20 metres to over 7 kilometres wide, and it cuts through the centre of the capital, Nicosia. Looked at on a map, it seems to be land between two countries, which is why it belongs in a study of places outside every country.

It began with a pencil line. After fighting between Greek and Turkish Cypriots at Christmas 1963, a British general, Peter Young, drew an agreed ceasefire line on a map with a green chinagraph pencil on 30 December 1963. The United Nations force took over in 1964. In July 1974, after a short-lived Greek Cypriot coup, Turkey invaded and took about 37 per cent of the island. A ceasefire followed on 16 August, and the Security Council backed a security zone that only United Nations forces could enter. Today the zone marks the limit of the Turkish advance. North of it is the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, which is largely unrecognised, and south of it is the Republic of Cyprus.

The strip is not empty. Four villages lie inside it. Their listed populations in 2021 were Athienou 9,721, Pyla 2,771, Troulloi 1,175 and Deneia 373, about 14,000 people in all. Pyla is known as one of the few villages left in Cyprus where Greek and Turkish Cypriots live side by side. Elsewhere, untouched areas have become refuges for plants and animals, and the Turkish army has built fences, walls, watchtowers and minefields on its northern side. Crossing was very limited until 2003, when the rules were relaxed after nearly 30 years, and a European Union regulation of 2004 ended the Republic of Cyprus's restrictions on crossings by EU citizens. In March 2021 Cyprus put up a barbed wire fence on part of the zone. In August 2023 police and soldiers from the Turkish-controlled north clashed with peacekeepers inside the zone at Pyla over unauthorised construction work. Bulldozers removed United Nations trucks, concrete bollards and barbed wire, and three peacekeepers were seriously injured. Turkey's president accused the force of bias against Turkish Cypriots, and the Security Council called the incident a violation of the status quo and condemned the assault.

In law the strip is not a territory of its own. The United Nations patrols it under a ceasefire and does not own or rule it as a state, and the claims of the governments on either side continue. Residents remain tied to one of those communities. No declaration of a separate state there is known, and it remains under United Nations patrol.
cyprus-buffer-zone-pyla.why: The '10,000' figure is not on the listed source, whose village table totals about 14,000 for 2021. Added the 2004 EU regulation and the August 2023 Pyla clash.

batmans-treaty.story:
Batman's Treaty was an 1835 attempt by British colonists to buy the land where Melbourne, Australia, now stands directly from its Aboriginal owners. It is considered the first and only documented time Europeans negotiated their presence directly with the traditional owners. To follow what happened, it helps to know the colonial rule. Britain treated all of Australia as Crown land. Settlers could get land only by grant from the government, and settlement was limited to certain approved districts. Port Phillip lay beyond them.

The Port Phillip Association was a group of sheep farmers based mostly in Van Diemen's Land (Tasmania), who wanted new pasture across the strait. John Batman and the lawyer Joseph Gellibrand had applied for a grant at Port Phillip in 1827 and been refused. In 1835 they tried another way. Gellibrand drew up a deed, a legal document transferring an interest in land, with a yearly tribute, and Batman sailed from Launceston on 10 May in a 23-ton schooner with seven Aboriginal men from New South Wales and a few others. They exchanged gifts with local people for about a week.

On 6 June he met eight Wurundjeri and Boonwurrung elders beside a stream, probably Merri Creek in what is now Northcote, though the place is disputed. For 600,000 acres he handed over 40 pairs of blankets, 42 tomahawks, 130 knives, 62 pairs of scissors, 40 looking glasses, 250 handkerchiefs, 18 shirts, 4 flannel jackets, 4 suits of clothes and 150 pounds of flour. Two days later Batman wrote in his journal that a spot on the river would be the place for a village, a line later called Melbourne's founding charter.

The deed's validity has been widely disputed. The marks Batman presented as the elders' signatures resemble marks commonly used by Aboriginal people from the Sydney area, so one of the men he brought may have made them. Batman, his Aboriginal companions and the elders did not share a language. It is almost certain the elders did not understand the deed, and they probably saw it as part of the gift exchanges of the previous days, which may have amounted to a ceremony allowing temporary access to land.

The objection from the government came quickly. On 26 August the Governor of New South Wales, Richard Bourke, proclaimed such agreements void against the rights of the Crown and declared anyone on Crown land without authority a trespasser. The Colonial Office in London approved this in October. It objected that Batman had bought from Aboriginal people, whom British colonists did not accept had any claim to land, and that he had bought for the Association instead of the Crown.

The legal point has lasted. If the Aboriginal owners could sell, the Crown's claim to all land would be in question. So the proclamation denied their title and the buyer's together. A purchase from the people on the ground counted for nothing, because the only government with police and courts did not accept it.
batmans-treaty.why: Added the dispute over the marks and over what the elders understood, which the listed source gives and the story left out.

benetton-patagonia.story:
The Italian clothing group Benetton is the largest private landowner in Argentina, holding about 970,000 hectares in Patagonia, the far south of the country, as ranch land. It bought the land in 1991 when it purchased the Compañía de Tierras Sud Argentino. That company dates from 1889, when the Argentine government gave land to 10 British citizens, 90,000 hectares each. The grant passed over the Mapuche people who lived there, many of whom ended up as labourers on the new ranches.

The case is on the map because it shows what buying land from a government does and does not buy. Benetton got ownership, and it has no government of its own there. Argentina's police and courts decide disputes, and those courts have treated the company's papers as decisive.

In 2002 a Mapuche couple, Atilio Curiñanco and Rosa Nahuelquir, moved with their children onto Santa Rosa, a 534-hectare part of the Leleque ranch, believing it was government land. The company complained, and police removed them and destroyed their home and crops. A judge cleared them of criminal blame, but ruled in the civil case that the land was Benetton's. In 2004 they travelled to Rome with the Nobel Peace laureate Adolfo Pérez Esquivel to meet Luciano Benetton, who promised to look for a solution.

He offered the Chubut provincial government 7,500 hectares elsewhere for Mapuche farming, and the province rejected it as unproductive. In February 2007, 25 Mapuche including six families occupied Santa Rosa again, saying it was their ancestral territory. In March 2011 Judge Omar Magallanes ruled for Benetton, gave the company the disputed land and ordered the residents to leave within 10 days. The community appealed. The company's own statement gives the ruling date as 21 February 2011 and says the courts then avoided ruling further because Law 26.160, Argentina's emergency law on Indigenous land possession, suspended evictions. It dates that law's expiry to 2017 and says it has since pressed its claim through institutional channels. How the appeal ended is not known.
benetton-patagonia.why: Added why the 2011 order was not carried out, attributed to the company. Note: the company's 2017 expiry date could not be cross-checked.

add_sources.t: Compañía de Tierras Sud Argentino, statement on occupations, Benetton Group

british-north-borneo-company.story:
The British North Borneo Company was a private company that ran what is now Sabah, a state of Malaysia on the island of Borneo, for over 60 years. It is one of the clearest cases of a business becoming a government. It began with a deal made by Baron von Overbeck, a German businessman and diplomat, and the brothers Alfred and Edward Dent, who headed a British trading firm in Shanghai and London. They wanted a colonial concession, meaning a grant of rights over the land.

On 29 December 1877 the Sultan of Brunei agreed to one for 15,000 Spanish dollars. It then emerged that Brunei had already given some of the area to the Sultan of Sulu, so a second agreement was signed with him on 22 January 1878 for 5,000 dollars a year, with help from a Scottish adventurer named William Cowie. Overbeck and the Dents thereby became rulers of the territory on paper. Overbeck left in 1879 after failing to interest Germany. Alfred Dent turned to Britain, set up a provisional company with £300,000 of capital, and on 1 November 1881 received a royal charter, its legal authority to operate.

The charter is what changed the deal from private paper into something other governments would respect. The company then did what a state does. It recruited Sikh policemen from northern India, set up courts and prisons, levied taxes and built a railway from Jesselton to Tenom. Its governor sat at Sandakan, with districts run by officers and even named after directors, such as Dent and Alcock. Its first settlement, on Gaya Island, was burnt in a raid by a local leader, Mat Salleh, and resistance to its taxes continued for years. After Cowie joined the board in 1894, the company was run largely from London with shareholder returns uppermost, and Dent resigned. Britain made the territory a protectorate in 1888, meaning Britain took charge of its foreign relations.

The Second World War ended it. The company could not pay for rebuilding, so on 26 June 1946 it handed North Borneo to the Colonial Office, the British government department for colonies, for £860,000 in cash. In 1949 an independent arbitrator, a person appointed to settle the dispute, awarded a further £1.4 million, which disappointed shareholders, and share prices fell by almost half. The territory joined Malaysia in 1963.

The argument over the first deal has outlasted the company. The Sulu paper has been read both as a sale and as a lease. Malaysia kept paying the yearly fee to the sultan's heirs until 2013. Heirs then went to private arbitration in Europe. A Madrid court annulled the appointment of the arbitrator, Gonzalo Stampa, in June 2021 because Malaysia had not been properly notified, and he moved the case to Paris. In February 2022 he held that Malaysia owed the heirs $14.92 billion. French courts held that he had no jurisdiction, and Malaysia won a final ruling in France's top court on 6 November 2024. A Spanish court found Stampa guilty of contempt of court and sentenced him to six months in prison, and a Madrid appeal court upheld that on 17 May 2024.
british-north-borneo-company.why: Added the figures and the arbitrator's conviction from the listed source.

casado-chaco.story:
The Chaco is a dry forest and scrub region covering western Paraguay. In the late 19th century the Paraguayan state sold off public land there. The Carlos Casado company, set up in Rosario, Argentina, was the biggest buyer of this kind. It acquired over 7,800 square kilometres in 1886 and came to hold more than 5 million hectares. It wanted quebracho, a tree whose wood yields tannin, a substance used for tanning hides.

The company then built what the state had not. It founded the town of Puerto Casado in 1889 on the Paraguay River and laid a narrow-gauge railway about 145 kilometres west into the forest. The founder's son, José Casado, came to manage it in 1929 and lived there until 1945. For a long time this was in effect a company town, with the owner's house, factory, port and rail line at its centre.

Paraguay still held the right to rule it. Mennonite settlers passed through from 1926 on company trains on their way to new colonies. When the Chaco War with Bolivia began, the port served as a military post, the commanding general lived in a house lent by the company, and the railway carried soldiers, supplies and wounded. Its workshops repaired the army's machinery.

The company stopped production in the late 1990s and its tannin factory is shut. In 2000 it sold about 240,000 hectares in Alto Paraguay, including part of the municipality with its residents still living there, to a group called the Moon Sect, after the Korean religious leader Sun Myung Moon, which acts through a company called Victoria. Local residents travelled nearly 600 kilometres to Asunción, partly on foot, to ask the government to expropriate the land, meaning take it over for public use. Earlier expropriation bills did not succeed. The group donated 30,000 hectares to the state in 2007, and by 2019 they had still not been registered in favour of Puerto Casado. In 2012 the national land institute declared about 35,000 hectares a settlement, then cancelled that decision. In May 2019 the town council voted 7 to 5 to back a new request to Congress covering 22,000 hectares. How that request ended is not known.
casado-chaco.why: Railway length is 145 km on the source. Removed 'Guaraní people', a misreading of a garbled source sentence. Added what happened after the sale, which the story left open.

add_sources.t: Nuevo intento de Puerto Casado para recuperar tierras de Secta Moon, Última Hora, 22 May 2019

congo-free-state.mechanism: A private person turned bundles of treaties with local leaders into a state by persuading outside powers to recognise it, meaning to accept it as a state. Public and diplomatic pressure over the abuses later led Belgium to annex it as a colony.
congo-free-state.why: Mechanism said the recognising powers took back what they had granted. The story itself says Belgium's parliament annexed the territory under pressure.

firestone-liberia.story:
In 1926 the American tyre maker Firestone won a 99-year lease on up to a million acres of Liberia, in West Africa, at six cents an acre, wherever in the country it chose. That was 4 per cent of Liberia's territory and nearly 10 per cent of its land then considered arable. Liberia was then the only independent country in its region, and it is on the map because it shows how a company can gain great power in a state without any change of borders.

Each side had a reason. Rubber was vital for car tyres, and Britain, then dominating world production, had restricted supply from 1922 under the Stevenson Plan. Harvey Firestone's response was the slogan that America must grow its own rubber. The American government helped search for sites. Liberia's government, for its part, wanted American protection from colonial neighbours eager to annex it.

After the legislature approved a draft, Firestone added a new clause requiring Liberia to take a $5 million loan from his own company, at 7 per cent. The terms matched a 1918 American loan proposal that had aroused objections in Liberia, where critics feared it would make the country an American-run territory, and the new clause set off wide protests. The stated purpose was to pay off more than a million dollars owed to British banks, which might otherwise give Britain a reason to interfere. Firestone also wanted political control to protect a long-term investment. He offered to build a port, which he did not need, to win over the State Department, which wanted one for naval use. Liberia agreed under pressure from the State Department. Two leading Liberian supporters of the bill, a former president and a senator, had by then been hired as Firestone's lawyers.

The terms went well beyond farming. An American financial adviser controlled Liberia's budget, and the country could not borrow without the written consent of Firestone's finance company. The company was largely exempted from present and future taxes. Liberia also promised to help it find labour, and since people in the interior were outside the money economy, this led to forced recruitment. Residents of Harbel were moved away, and in 1929 a local king complained to the legislature that nine towns had been destroyed and that people had to choose between forced labour and emigration.

By 1932 the loan took nearly all government revenue. When Liberia missed a payment, Firestone asked the American government to send a warship, and President Roosevelt refused. So the company could press a government and lobby its own, while force stayed in the hands of the American government, which declined to use it.

Liberia never lost its formal independence. One account calls the result an American protectorate in practice, meaning a country controlled by a stronger one. The 99-year term did not end the arrangement. In February 2005, after 14 years of civil war, Liberia's transitional government extended the concession by a further 36 years, subject to ratification by parliament, while the company, by then part of Bridgestone, promised more than $100 million of investment, much of it for replanting trees. Critics in Margibi county, where the plantation lies, objected that a transitional government should not commit the country beyond its own mandate, and that the company had built little for the people living there. An amended agreement was signed in 2008. The company still runs the world's largest contiguous rubber farm, at Harbel.
firestone-liberia.why: Story stopped at 1932 for the lease. Added the 2005 extension and 2008 amendment, so a reader does not assume the 99 years ran out in 2025. The 2008 item rests on a trade-press headline only.

add_sources.t: Deal could mark return of private investors, IRIN, 22 Feb 2005
Liberia, BFS sign amended rubber concession agreement, European Rubber Journal, 26 Feb 2008

golden-triangle-kings-romans.story:
The Golden Triangle Special Economic Zone is a casino and hotel district on the Mekong River in Bokeo Province, Laos, run by a private company on a long lease. It lies where Laos, Myanmar and Thailand meet, directly across the river from a Thai village. Farmland stood there before, and the people of the village of Ban Kwan were moved to make way.

A special economic zone is an area where a government applies lighter rules to attract investment. In 2007 the Hong Kong-registered Kings Romans Group and the Lao government created this one with the aim of developing a poor region. The company took a 99-year lease on 10,000 hectares, with 3,000 hectares set aside as a duty-free zone.

It draws mostly Chinese visitors. Mandarin is widely spoken, the clocks are set to Beijing time and the Chinese yuan is the usual currency, so some have labelled it a Chinese colony in all but name. The company runs ferries from Thailand, has its own immigration checkpoint on Lao soil and shops, a hospital and apartment blocks. In 2024 the province and the zone's owner, Zhao Wei, opened a new international airport. Bokeo has gone from one of the country's poorest provinces to one of its better off.

In January 2018 the United States Treasury imposed sanctions on the company and on Zhao Wei, accusing them of money laundering and of drug, human and animal trafficking. Zhao Wei denies the accusations. In 2023 the United Kingdom, Canada and the United States announced further sanctions naming Zhao Wei, citing United Nations reports linking him to forced labour and trafficking through online scams, which he also denies. In 2024 Chinese and Lao police carried out joint raids on call-centre fraud gangs in the zone, and early in 2025 Laos's Ministry of Public Security declared that none remained. Shipments of drugs are still reported to pass nearby.

The zone still operates. On paper it is leased land within Laos, under Lao sovereignty, and no declaration of independence has been made.
golden-triangle-kings-romans.why: Replaced vague 'some enforcement action' with the 2023 sanctions, 2024 raids and 2025 Lao declaration.

add_sources.t: Spotlight on Zhao Wei after KK Park scam crackdown in Myanmar, The Star, 29 Oct 2025

greenland-purchase-offers.story:
The United States has tried several times to buy Greenland, the Arctic island that belongs to the Kingdom of Denmark and governs itself. Buying territory from another state has real precedents, including the American purchase of Alaska in 1867.

Secretary of State William Seward backed a purchase in 1867, the same year as Alaska, and there were talks again in 1910. In 1946 the United States secretly offered Denmark $100 million in gold, which Denmark rejected. In 2019 President Trump said he wanted to buy the island, and Danish prime minister Mette Frederiksen called the idea absurd and said Greenland was not for sale.

In his second term from 2025 Trump pressed again and spoke of tariffs against Denmark. In January 2026 Greenland's leader Jens-Frederik Nielsen said Greenland would choose Denmark, and reports put opposition to an American takeover at 85 percent of Greenlanders.

The law has changed since the earlier offers. An offer in 1946 went to the Danish government. Under Greenland's Self-Government Act, independence is for the Greenlandic people to decide, followed by negotiation with Denmark and a referendum. So a sale over the heads of the people living there would run against the law that governs the island.

On 22 September 2026 the United States, Denmark and Greenland signed a security agreement in New York with no expiry date. It expands the American military presence and bars countries outside NATO, the Western military alliance, from setting up military installations, and it says Greenland would remain in NATO if it became independent. Frederiksen said it recognises Denmark's sovereignty, meaning its legal right to rule the island, and the Greenlandic people's right to decide their own future. No sale has taken place.

The agreement gave the United States a larger military presence with no change of ownership.
greenland-purchase-offers.why: Added a term of the 2026 agreement given in the listed source.

herm-lease.story:
Herm is a tiny island in the Channel Islands, about a mile and a half long, part of the Bailiwick of Guernsey, a self-governing territory under the British Crown. It is on the map because its right of use has been traded for nearly 300 years, while the ownership stayed with a government.

A lease is a right to use land for a fixed time in return for payment, and when the time runs out the land goes back to the owner. The Crown first leased it in 1737 to a Guernsey farmer, Peter Carey, for 61 years at £14 a year, and the lease then changed hands many times, for £7,500 by 1884. Prince Gebhard Blücher, a German noble, took it in 1889 and brought in wallabies, which lasted until 1910. The British government made him leave at the outbreak of war in 1914. The novelist Compton Mackenzie took over the tenancy in 1920 and recalled numerous practical problems during his three years there. Percival Perry was tenant from 1923 to 1939. During the Second World War German troops used the beaches for practice landings and left little behind.

The States of Guernsey, the island's government, bought Herm from the Crown so that local people and tourists could enjoy it, for £15,000 on 29 July 1946 according to one passage of Wikipedia's article and in 1949 according to another. It let the island to Major Peter Wood in 1949, who restored the run-down island with his wife over 30 years. In 2008 his daughter and her husband put the remaining 40 years of their lease up for sale, asking £15 million. A trust called Starboard Settlement bought it for considerably less and formed Herm Island Ltd to run the island.

Talks on a 21-year extension broke down in 2013, with the tenant offering £440,000 and the States of Guernsey asking for £6 million. In 2023 the lease was extended to 2069 for an undisclosed sum, and Herm Island Ltd still runs the island. Throughout all of this Guernsey's laws applied and its government stayed the landlord, so no buyer ever gained any right to govern.
herm-lease.why: The lease trade began in 1737, not 1889. Blücher's tenancy ended in 1914. The source gives both 1946 and 1949 for the purchase.

huang-nubo-grimsstadir.story:
In 2011 Huang Nubo, a Chinese businessman who founded the property firm Zhongkun Group, tried to buy about 300 square kilometres of wilderness at Grímsstaðir á Fjöllum in north-eastern Iceland, equal to 0.3 per cent of the country. He offered about $10 million for the land, which was partly owned by the government, and planned to spend about $200 million on a tourist resort and what he described as Europe's biggest nature reserve. Iceland was then recovering from its financial crisis, and some saw the investment as useful outside the capital region.

Icelandic law bars large land purchases by people or companies from outside the European Economic Area, a group of European countries that share a single market. So he needed an exemption from the minister. Interior Minister Ögmundur Jónasson refused in late 2011. He said an exemption would make the law meaningless and could encourage others to buy up large parts of Iceland, and he stressed that the buyer was a company, Huang's Zhongkun. Parties split, with the Social Democrats leaning toward the deal and the minister's Left Greens opposed. One Social Democrat member of parliament called the decision crazy, deplorable and devastating, and said there were at least 25 precedents.

Huang called the minister a racist. In May 2012 a committee of three ministries recommended a smaller deal, a 40-year lease of two to three square kilometres for a hotel and tourist facilities. Huang had said that building one hotel did not interest him. That 40-year lease attempt also failed. In December 2016 it was reported that Jim Ratcliffe, a British billionaire and majority shareholder of the Ineos chemical group, had bought the largest portion of Grímsstaðir, which had been listed for sale since October at 780 million krónur, about €6.55 million. The head of an angling club said the purchase was part of a salmon project for rivers in the north-east and that Ratcliffe had no plans to use the land. Ögmundur Jónasson, the minister who had opposed the sale to Huang, said he was disappointed. Britain was then in the European Economic Area, so the rule that had stopped Huang did not apply in the same way.

The bid never touched the question of who rules the land, since a buyer would have held it under Icelandic law. It shows that a state can stop a sale at the earlier stage, by controlling who may own land at all.
huang-nubo-grimsstadir.why: Outcome was given as unknown. The lease failed, and the land went to Jim Ratcliffe in 2016.

add_sources.t: Grímsstaðir á Fjöllum geht an Briten, Iceland Review, Dec 2016

palmyra-fullard-leo.story:
Palmyra is an uninhabited coral atoll in the central Pacific, about 1,000 miles south of Hawaii, made up of 33 islets with about 600 acres of dry land and a large submerged reef. It has been bought and sold by private owners while also being claimed by governments, which makes it a good place to see that owning land and ruling it are two separate things.

American visitors tried to claim it in 1859 under the Guano Islands Act, a law on claiming islands that hold guano, or bird droppings, used as fertiliser. It had none, so the claims were abandoned. In 1862 King Kamehameha IV of Hawaii commissioned two Hawaiian citizens, Zenas Bent and Johnson Wilkinson, to take possession. The Kingdom of Hawaii annexed it on 15 April and the two became its joint owners. So one act gave a kingdom the right to rule and gave two men the ownership. Their shares were then sold and inherited many times, through a widow's four heirs, a navigation company and others. In 1922 Henry Cooper sold his interest to Leslie and Ellen Fullard-Leo for $15,000, and they set up a company to harvest coconuts.

The atoll came under the United States when Hawaii did. The family tried from 1937 to lease it to the Navy, but during the talks the federal government sued them, claiming that the atoll had never been lawfully private property. The Navy occupied it and built a runway during the Second World War. The case reached the US Supreme Court as United States v. Fullard-Leo, and in 1947 the Court ruled for the Fullard-Leo and Cooper families, which confirmed their private title against the government. This did not make Palmyra independent of the United States in any way. The government that lost as a claimant to ownership remained the government.

It is now the only incorporated US territory, meaning one fully under the Constitution and permanently American, with no resident government. The Interior Department administers it.

The family later turned down offers to use the atoll as a nuclear waste dump or a casino, according to the Nature Conservancy, a conservation charity, which bought most of the land from them in 2000 for $30 million. The southwestern islets, including Home, still belong to descendants of Henry Cooper and others. The rest of Palmyra is a federal wildlife refuge, and researchers work there in a station the charity opened in 2005.
palmyra-fullard-leo.why: The sale in 2000 did not cover the whole atoll. Private owners remain.

sazan-kushner.story:
Sazan is Albania's largest island, a strip of rock in the Adriatic Sea about 4.8 km long and 2 km wide, with an area of 5.7 square kilometres. It sits between the Strait of Otranto and the Bay of Vlorë, where the Adriatic meets the Ionian Sea, and that position has made it valuable to armies. For decades Albania's then-ally the Soviet Union used it as a submarine base and as a testing ground for biological and chemical weapons, and Soviet-era gas masks still lie around the island. It remains a designated military exclusion zone, nobody lives there, and it has been open to the public only since July 2015.

Across the water is Zvërnec, a strip of beach and cliffs that shelters an inland lagoon. It belongs to a protected area called Vjosa-Narta, where the ornithologist Taulant Bino and his colleagues have recorded about 250 bird species, including flamingos and breeding terns.

Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump, the son-in-law and daughter of US President Donald Trump, want to build a luxury resort here. Ivanka Trump said in a 2026 podcast that they found Sazan years ago while on a friend's boat, swam ashore and hiked to the top. She described both the island and about five miles of beachfront opposite it as theirs. Bino says the project ideas he has seen show tall buildings and up to 10,000 rooms, which he describes as a new city.

The legal path ran through Albania's parliament. Land in a protected area normally cannot be used this way. Dorian Matlija, a lawyer for a group of environmental organizations, says the area's rules allow only traditional farming and fishing. In 2024 Prime Minister Edi Rama's government passed a law that removed the area's protection and allowed five-star hotels, and the government has given the resort preliminary approval. The environmental groups have gone to court. They argue that the law breaks Albanian law and also the rules of Natura 2000, the European Union's network of protected nature sites, which they say bind Albania because it is a candidate to join the EU.

Construction crews built an access road into the protected area during the breeding season. In June 2026 thousands protested outside the prime minister's office in Tirana for days on end, and hundreds gathered on the beach itself. Some said that the government was selling land that was not its to sell.

The money is hard to trace. On 2 June 2026 anti-corruption prosecutors froze the bank accounts of Albania Land Development, a firm owned by the Qatari brothers Moutaz and Ramez Al-Khayyat, who are helping to finance and build the resort, as part of an inquiry into fraudulent property titles. A representative said that Kushner's investment firm, Affinity Partners, has no role and that partners invest in their personal capacity. The investigative journalist Lindita Cela followed the ownership through a chain of shell companies, firms with no real business of their own, from Albania to the Netherlands. Several shared one Amsterdam address and were each worth a single euro.

Who owned the land is also in dispute. In April 2026 a Miami-based businessman, Artur Shehu, sold the coastal strip to Albania Land Development, which Reuters describes as owned by the developer, Sazan Real Estate Development, and other investors. Case files reviewed by Reuters in July 2026 show that Albania's organised crime agency suspects Shehu's deeds were forged, and prosecutors have issued a warrant for his arrest for laundering drug money. His lawyer denies all of it. The files make no allegation of wrongdoing against Kushner, the developer or other investors. Sazan says Kushner is an investor and that it believes the land purchases were legitimate. Villagers from Zvërnec have contested Shehu's claim in court for more than a decade, and their lawyer said they would seek an order halting the project. The government says it will not intervene in private transactions and that the project complies with Albanian and EU law.

Nothing here makes Sazan a separate country. Albania keeps the right to make and enforce law on the island and the beach, and a buyer gets only what Albanian law allows. The case shows the limit of that position for anyone hoping to build a private enclave. The permission rests on one government's statute, and the same courts, prosecutors and voters can reopen it. As of mid-2026 the resort is not finished, and the court cases and the title inquiry are unresolved.
sazan-kushner.why: Added the July 2026 Reuters report on suspected forged deeds and the villagers' title suit. Sources also differ on who owns Albania Land Development: NPR says the Al-Khayyat brothers, Reuters says Sazan and other investors.

add_sources.t: Businessman who sold land for Kushner resort in Albania suspected of faking the deeds, Reuters via The Star, 11 Jul 2026
